RAZI, d. 606 (author): Known bodily benefits are only a drop in the ocean of the unknown; understanding divine wisdom in creating the human being involves ten thousand questions or more. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (author): Al-Anʿām’s praise for creating the heavens, earth, darkness, and light is one subset of Rabb al-ʿālamīn; dependence on God for preservation entails dependence for origination. | mentions 6:1 RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (author): The Prophet identifies al-Fatiha as a surah unmatched in the Torah, Gospel, or Psalms; the Companions' answer about what they recite in prayer indicates a known universal practice. [RAZI-FULL:v1p158#2/ r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi argues that Quran 73:20 requires al-Fatiha: the options are al-Fatiha, another surah, or a choice; the latter two fail because another is not universally required and al-Fatiha is agreed better and more complete. | mentions 73:20 RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (author): A giver who seeks reward, praise, repayment, or release from stinginess seeks compensation and is not the true benefactor; God gives from intrinsic fullness. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (author): Worldly blessings are finite, but the praise phrase is infinite; what remains after accounting for a finite blessing is endless, warranting eternal reward. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (author): The phrase should be reserved for the best blessings: religious benefits outrank worldly ones, inner acts outrank bodily acts, and seeing a worldly benefit as the giver’s gift is nobler than treating it merely as a benefit. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (author): They further argue that if God is praised intrinsically, no act causes that entitlement, so no duty, compensation, or reward is owed; if it is not intrinsic, God would depend on another. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (المعتزلة): The Muʿtazila say absolute praise is deserved by one whose acts contain no evil, rulings no injustice, and judgments no oppression; they reject the Jabriyya picture of God creating disbelief then punishing it. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (author): Created nurturers seek their own profit, such as reward or praise, while God nurtures for the creatures’ benefit rather than His own. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (author): The Prophet's constant practice makes abandoning his command forbidden, and Muslims agree that the Fatiha is better and more complete than another recitation. | mentions 24:63 QURTUBI, d. 671 (author): Abu ʿAbd Allah explains that the person first receives the world and then the enduring word of praise, which is better because the world perishes while the word remains among the righteous deeds. | mentions 18:46 QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ابن عطية): Ibn ʿAtiyya chooses the monotheistic formula, citing the report that it is the best utterance of the Prophet and earlier prophets. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): Anas reports that God is pleased when a servant praises Him after eating a meal or drinking. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أبو عبد الله): Abu ʿAbd Allah explains that the enduring word is better because the world perishes, while praise remains among the righteous deeds; both world and praise ultimately come from God. | mentions 18:46 BAYDAWI, d. 685 (author): If the article is exhaustive, all praise belongs to God because He bestows every good directly or indirectly; this implies He is living, powerful, willing, and knowing. | mentions 16:53 BAYDAWI, d. 685 (author): Readings assimilate dāl and lām in opposite directions, treating the letters as one word because they are used together. BAYDAWI, d. 685 (author): Shukr is broader than ḥamd and madh in one respect and narrower in another; praise is a branch of gratitude and better signals blessings than hidden belief or ambiguous bodily acts, so it is gratitude's chief element. BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 (author): Two recitations assimilate the dāl and lām in either direction, treating them as one word because the terms are used together. QASHANI, d. 736 (author): God is owner at the final return and recompense; only the worshipped one to whom sovereignty returns can reward enduring blessing for perishable life, as servants shed acts and attributes and receive true existence after annihilation. ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 (ابن الأعرابي): Ibn al-Aʿrābī records the plural aḥmad for ḥamd, apparently treating its different kinds as distinct, and cites a poem using aḥmadī. SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 (author): The accusative may alternatively be a direct object of recite or read, but the verbal-noun analysis is better because the wording itself supports it. SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 (author): Hamd praises beauty whether or not a favor was bestowed and is expressed only by the tongue; shukr is for a received favor and may be by heart, tongue, or limbs. | mentions 34:13 SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 (author): Views range from treating hamd and shukr as synonymous, to making hamd absolutely broader, to distinguishing praise of attributes from thanks for acts. IBNKATHIR, d. 774 (author): Ibn Kathir questions Ibn Jarir's equation: praise is verbal commendation for necessary or bestowed qualities, while thanks applies only to bestowed qualities and may be inward, spoken, or enacted. IBNKATHIR, d. 774 (author): Ibn Kathir resolves the scope dispute by saying praise covers more kinds of objects but is speech-only, whereas thanks uses more kinds of means but concerns bestowed qualities alone. IBNKATHIR, d. 774 (الجوهري): Al-Jawhari defines thanks as praising a benefactor for what he bestowed and says using the preposition li- is more eloquent. IBNKATHIR, d. 774 (author): Ibn Kathir distinguishes praise from eulogy: eulogy can concern living or dead people and even objects, precede or follow a favor, and address necessary or bestowed qualities. IBNKATHIR, d. 774 (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): The Companion al-Aswad ibn Sari asks to recite praises of his Lord, and the Prophet replies that his Lord loves praise. BURHAN, d. 794 (ابن حبان): Ibn Hibban reads the report comparing al-Fatiha with the Torah and Gospel as a difference in reward granted by God’s favor, not as intrinsic superiority within the Quran. DURR, d. 911 (رسول الله): When al-Aswad ibn Sariʿ offers the Prophet praises he composed for God, the Prophet replies that his Lord loves praise; al-Hakim authenticates the report.
